168.subtitle: Above the categories, and made of them

commentary.meaning: Six names, and the first three all begin with the same four letters — except that the third one does not, and the whole verse turns on noticing it. The opening pair state a contradiction and do not soften it: she stands above the principles by which the cosmos is counted out, and she is made of those principles. The third name then resolves the contradiction by a change of cut. Read the same syllables not as tattva, thatness, but as tat and tvam, that and thou, and what you have is the two words of the Upaniṣadic sentence in which the self and the absolute are declared to be one thing. A puzzle about cosmology turns out to be a statement about identity. Then the verse changes register entirely and gives three names that could belong to a person: she likes a particular kind of singing, she is gentle, and she keeps house with Sadāśiva. The word for the last is the plainest one available, the ordinary term for the woman who runs a household.
commentary.history:
Tattva is a made word and a rather awkward one. It is the pronoun tat, that, with the abstract suffix -tva added to it, so its literal sense is thatness — the state of being that. Sanskrit uses it for truth, for reality, for the essence of a thing, and above all for an item in a numbered list of the constituents of the world. Which list depends on the school. Classical Sāṃkhya counts twenty-five, from puruṣa and prakṛti down through intellect, ego, mind, the eleven faculties, the five subtle elements and the five gross ones. The Śaiva systems keep those twenty-five, treat them as the impure end of the scale, and add eleven more above them, running up through māyā and its five constraining sheaths to śuddhavidyā, īśvara, sadāśiva, śakti and śiva: thirty-six in all. The number is not decoration. A tattva scheme is a map of how consciousness becomes a world, read downward, and of how a practitioner retraces the descent, read upward.

The first two names take the two available positions on such a map and refuse to choose between them. Adhikā governs an ablative — greater than, in excess of, over and above the tattvas — and it places her outside the scheme, at the point where counting stops. Mayī, the feminine of the suffix -maya, means consisting of, made out of, and it places her inside every item counted. This pairing is the oldest move in Indian theology and the stotra has made it before, but it lands differently here, thirty names from the end, because by now the reader has watched the hymn do it perhaps forty times. Whatever it says she is beyond, it will say in the next breath that she is.

The third name is a pun that the tradition takes entirely seriously. Written out, tattvamartha looks like tattva with a stray -m before artha. It is not. The commentators generally read the first member as tat tvam, the fragment of the sentence tat tvam asi, that thou art, which Uddālaka repeats to his son Śvetaketu nine times in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. So the name says that her own form is the meaning of that sentence: not that she teaches the identity of self and absolute, and not that she exemplifies it, but that she is what the sentence is about. A minority reading keeps tattvam as one word and takes artha in the sense of purpose, giving something like she whose nature is the goal of all the principles; the two readings are not far apart in effect, and the first is much the commoner. It is worth noticing what the poet has done technically. Three names in a row open on the same syllables, and the third one only pretends to. Sanskrit compounding, which normally blurs the seams between words, is being used here to hide a sentence inside a noun.

Then the register drops. Sāmagānapriyā names the Sāmaveda, the collection whose verses are almost all borrowed from the Ṛgveda and whose distinctive content is not words but melody: how the borrowed verses are stretched, repeated, broken and fitted with meaningless syllables called stobhas in order to be sung. It is the one Veda that cannot be printed adequately, because what it consists of is a performance. To say that this singing is what she loves, in a hymn composed in the plainest of metres and recited rather than sung, is a small act of deference from one kind of sacred speech to another. Kṛṣṇa makes the same ranking in the tenth chapter of the Gītā when he names the Sāmaveda as his own among the four.

Saumyā is the adjective from soma, and it carries the moon with it, since soma is the moon as well as the pressed plant of the Vedic rite. The dictionary range runs from lunar and cool through mild, placid and benign, and in classical prose the vocative saumya is simply the polite way to address a man you are being kind to, roughly good sir. After the metaphysics of the first line, the word is almost startlingly ordinary.

Sadāśiva is a technical name, not a synonym for Śiva. In the thirty-six-tattva scheme he stands third from the top, below śiva and śakti and above īśvara, at the level where the universe about to be emitted is still felt as a vague I-am-this rather than as an object. He is also the fifth of the five brahmans whose corpse-couch this hymn has already described, and he will return in that role six verses further on. What the stotra pairs with that exceedingly abstract figure is kuṭumbinī: kuṭumba is a household, a family, the people and property that make up a domestic establishment, and kuṭumbin is the man who has one. The feminine is his wife. It is the vocabulary of the household register, and it is the last word of a verse that began at the top of the tattva scheme.
commentary.practice:
The first line is a trap of the kind that catches experienced reciters. Three names in a row begin tattva-, tattva-, tattva-, and the third is longer than the first two put together. What goes wrong is not mispronunciation but arithmetic: one of the three gets said twice, or one gets dropped, and nothing in the sound tells you. Fix the line by its logic rather than by its music. Above, made of, and then the sentence — beyond the list, inside the list, and then the reason both can be true.

The cluster is ttv, and it is three articulations with no vowel anywhere in them: a dental t held closed, a second dental t released, and then v, which in Sanskrit is made with the lower lip against the upper teeth and is softer than an English v. Say tat, then tva, as two distinct movements, and only then run them together. The commonest fault is to reduce the double t to a single one, which turns tattva into a word that does not exist.

The join in the first name is worth seeing because it is the most frequent sandhi in the language: tattva ends in short a, adhikā begins with short a, and two short a sounds fuse into one long ā. So the long vowel in the middle of tattvādhikā is a seam. The same rule, run twice, is what produces the long vowels in several of the names later in this stretch of the hymn.

In the third name, the syllable that separates the two readings is the -m of tattvam, and it is exactly one consonant. Give it its full value. If it is swallowed the name collapses back into the first two and the pun is lost, which in this case means the doctrine is lost.

Sāmagānapriyā rests the line. Two long ās, no conjunct except pr, and the r after p is a single tap of the tongue-tip, not the American approximant. Saumyā, by contrast, is dense: au is a full-length diphthong and not the short glide of English how, and my is a labial m running straight into a palatal y with no vowel between them.

Sadāśivakuṭumbinī is eight syllables and only two of them need care. The ś of śiva is the palatal sibilant, made with the tongue flat against the hard palate, and it is not the retroflex ṣ. The ṭ of kuṭumbinī is retroflex, tongue-tip curled back, and it sits between two labials; the mb that follows is a nasal into its own voiced stop, which English handles without difficulty.

In archanā the six names take the dative, and this verse hands you both of the endings you need. Tattvādhikā is an ā-stem and gives tattvādhikāyai namaḥ; tattvamayī is an ī-stem and gives tattvamayyai namaḥ, with the ī turning into the glide y before the ending. The two stand side by side at the head of the line, which makes this a good place to fix the difference by ear.

What to hold while chanting it: the verse spends half its length establishing that she cannot be located on any map of reality and the other half describing a household. Neither half is a concession to the other.

169.subtitle: Both paths, and the steadiness they ask for

commentary.meaning: Six names in two clean halves, and the halves do different work. The first line is about routes and about danger: she stands on the left-hand way and the right-hand way alike, and she turns aside every calamity. The second line stops saying what she does for anyone and says what she is — settled in herself, sweet by constitution rather than by effort, steady, and worshipped by the steady. The hinge is the third name, svasthā, which in ordinary Sanskrit means nothing loftier than being well. Set immediately after a name about the averting of disaster, it makes a quiet correction: what she has to give is not a series of rescues but the condition she is already in. And the verse ends by naming her worshippers, which the hymn rarely does. The ones it names are not the ardent or the learned. They are the composed.
commentary.history:
Savya means left and apasavya is built by negating it, not on the ordinary word for right. Before either term had anything to do with tantric schools, both were terms of Vedic ritual practice describing where a cord sits and which way a man walks. The sacrificial thread worn over the left shoulder and under the right arm is the normal arrangement, used for rites directed at the gods; reversed, over the right shoulder, it marks the rites for the ancestors, and the ritual manuals call that reversal by the name that appears in this compound. Circumambulation works the same way, clockwise with the right side to the object for auspicious occasions and counter-clockwise for funerary ones. So the first name of this verse begins its life describing two positions of a piece of string, and two directions of walking, both of them entirely orthodox.

On top of that the tantric traditions laid the distinction that modern readers usually meet first: the right-hand observance and the left-hand one, dakṣiṇācāra and vāmācāra. What the distinction actually amounts to is narrower than the popular account suggests. Both wings work with the same deities, the same diagram and largely the same liturgy. What separates them is whether the rite is performed with substances and acts that ordinary purity rules exclude, or performed inwardly with those elements replaced by their contemplative equivalents. The vocabulary in the primary sources is looser than the textbooks, and different texts draw the line in different places. Śrīvidyā itself has never settled the question internally: it contains lineages that keep the whole rite interior and Brahminically pure and lineages that do not, and the two have argued for centuries. The stotra's response is to decline the argument. It says she is standing on both roads, and two verses later it will say the same thing again in the other pair of words.

Āpad, in the second name, is a formation from ā-√pad, to fall upon: a calamity is something that comes down on you. The prefixes on the verb pile up in the opposite direction — vi-ni-vāraṇa, a holding back, a warding off, from √vṛ. This is one of a small group of names near the end of the thousand that promise something specific to the reciter, and they cluster here because the phalaśruti is coming; the hymn is beginning to make explicit the transaction it has so far only implied. How to take such a promise is a fair question and the tradition has an answer, though it is a chastened one: the commentators generally read the averting of calamity as a change in the person to whom calamities happen rather than as a guarantee about events. The very next name is evidence that this is not special pleading, because it substitutes a description of her own state for anything she might be expected to do.

Svasthā is sva, one's own or one's self, plus the root √sthā, to stand. In medical and ordinary usage svastha means healthy, comfortable, at ease — the abstract noun svāsthya is the standard word for health — and the sense is that of a person who is where he belongs. The philosophical schools took the same image and made it technical: liberation is repeatedly described as standing in one's own form. The Yoga tradition's definition of the final state uses exactly that phrase. So the name manages to be simultaneously the humblest word in the verse and one of the largest claims in it, which is a trick this hymn performs often enough to be a signature.

Dhīra, twice at the end, is from dhī, thought or insight, and the adjective covers a range that English cannot hold in one word: steady, constant, resolute, deep, wise, grave. The Upaniṣads use it of the person who can tell the good from the merely pleasant, which is a matter of discrimination and of nerve at once. The handbooks of dramaturgy use it as the base term for their classification of heroes, dividing them into the dhīra who is exalted, the dhīra who is violent, the dhīra who is playful and the dhīra who is calm — four temperaments sharing one quality of not being blown about. When the last name of the verse says she is thoroughly worshipped by the dhīra, it is naming a qualification for this practice that is neither birth nor learning nor fervour. Sam-arcitā, with the prefix that means completely and together, suggests worship carried through rather than begun, which is the same virtue described from the outside.
commentary.practice:
Four names in a row begin with s and the last two begin with dh, and the change of consonant is the structure of the verse. If you can hear the line as four then two, you will not lose your place, which is the real risk in the first half: savya, sarva, sva, sva, four openings so alike that the ear stops distinguishing them.

The first name contains a sandhi that carries its whole meaning. Savya ends in short a and apasavya begins with short a, and two short a sounds fuse into a single long ā. So the long vowel in savyāpasavya is the seam between left and right, and a reciter who shortens it has deleted the negative prefix and left the goddess standing on one road. This is the same rule you met in the previous verse at tattvādhikā, and it is worth recognising both times.

Savya also gives the cluster vy: the labiodental v straight into the palatal glide y. Say it as one movement, not as v-uh-ya. The same cluster returns in the second half of the compound, so the word gives you two attempts at it in nine syllables.

Sarvāpadvinivāriṇī has the join dv, a voiced dental into a v, and then a small grammatical marvel at the end. The suffix is -in with the feminine ī, and the n has become retroflex ṇ because of the r earlier in the word. Sanskrit turns a dental n into a retroflex ṇ when certain sounds precede it in the same word, and r is the commonest trigger. The rule is worth knowing because it explains a dozen names in this hymn where a ṇ appears for no visible reason, including taruṇa in the next verse and kāruṇya elsewhere.

Svasthā is two syllables and four consonants. Sv is a dental sibilant into that soft v; sth is the same sibilant into an aspirated dental t, where the aspiration is a puff of breath released after the stop and not the English th of think. Take the word slowly enough that both clusters are audible, then say it at speed and see whether they survive.

Dhīrā opens with a single sound, not two. Dh is a voiced dental stop with breath released through it, and the temptation for an English speaker is to produce d followed by a separate h. Set the tongue for d, and let the release be breathy. Then the long ī, then a tapped r. The word occurs twice at the end of the verse, in dhīrā and again at the head of dhīrasamarcitā, which makes the close of the line the best drill in the verse for that one consonant.

In archanā the datives are straightforward: savyāpasavyamārgasthāyai namaḥ, sarvāpadvinivāriṇyai namaḥ, svasthāyai namaḥ, and so on. The ā-stems take -āyai and the two ī-stems, vinivāriṇī and nothing else here, take -yai. Note how much longer the first name becomes in the dative, and give it room.

What to hold while chanting it: the verse offers protection in its second name and then spends the whole of its second half describing a temperament. The order is not accidental. What it recommends is not that you should stop meeting trouble but that you should meet it the way she does.

170.subtitle: Consciousness poured out as the guest-water

commentary.meaning: Two names that empty out the rite and three that describe the person it is offered to. The first pair take the two most elementary articles of Indian worship — the water given to a guest on arrival and the flower laid before the image — and replace both with awareness. Nothing else about the rite changes. The vessel is still lifted, the gesture is still made, the words are still said; only the substance is different. Then the verse turns and gives three names that explain why such an offering could be accepted at all. She has risen and does not set. She is already satisfied, so that nothing brought to her can be a supplement. And her colour is that of the sun in the first minute after it clears the horizon. The last name is a portrait, and it is also the argument, because a sun that has just come up is the one thing in the visible world that looks like what the third name describes.
commentary.history:
Arghya is a technical term of hospitality before it is a term of worship. It comes from argha, worth or value, and behind that the root √argh, to be worth — the same family that gives arh, to deserve. The arghya is the valuable thing, the water offered in a small vessel to a guest of standing the moment he arrives, before he is seated and before anything else is done for him. Ritual worship simply treats the deity as such a guest, which is why the standard sequence of sixteen services begins with a seat, then water for the feet, then the arghya, and only much later reaches incense and lamps. In the Śrīvidyā rite a special vessel of arghya water is prepared and consecrated near the start of the sequence, and it becomes the medium through which most of what follows is offered. To say that her arghya is consciousness is therefore not a vague gesture at inwardness. It names the one article in the liturgy that everything else is poured from.

The second name does the same thing to the flower, and together they invoke the practice of interior worship, antaryāga, set against the outward rite performed with physical materials. The claim that inner worship is the higher of the two is very widely made in tantric literature, and it is worth being careful about what the texts actually do with it. In most schools, including this one, the internalising does not abolish the external rite; it doubles it. The practitioner performs the outward sequence and simultaneously performs an inward one, and the two are held together. There is a much-quoted verse listing the flowers of the inner worship — non-injury first, then restraint of the senses, compassion, patience, knowledge, austerity, meditation and truth — which circulates in devotional anthologies and is attributed to several different sources without agreement; it states the idea neatly, and its uncertain provenance is a reasonable warning against treating the idea as the property of any one text.

Caitanya is the abstract noun made from cetana, sentient, by lengthening the first vowel: the state of being conscious, consciousness as such. It is a plainer and later word than cit, which this hymn uses in its fourth name and again at the couch of corpses, and it is the standard term in the philosophical prose of the period. Choosing it here rather than cit keeps the two names sounding like ritual instructions rather than like metaphysics, which is the tone the verse wants: this is a rubric, not a meditation.

Sadoditā compresses sadā, always, and uditā, risen, and the compound is doing more than praising her constancy. Udita, arisen, has a technical life in the Śaiva philosophical vocabulary, where it is paired with śānta, quiescent, to distinguish the manifest state of a power from its resting state; a power described as perpetually udita is one that has no resting state to fall back into. Set against the ordinary sun, which is the standard example of something that rises, the name is a denial rather than a compliment: what makes a sunrise beautiful is that it is temporary, and she is being distinguished from it in exactly that respect. The tradition makes the same point elsewhere with the moon, where fifteen digits wax and wane and a sixteenth never does.

Sadātuṣṭā raises the question that every theology of worship has to answer. If she is always content, what is the rite for? The answer the tradition gives is not that the offering completes her but that it completes the offerer, and this verse has already arranged its own version of that answer: the arghya is consciousness, and consciousness is the one thing the worshipper has that was not brought in from outside. Read in that order, the five names make a single argument. Nothing you can pour out of a vessel will add to someone who is already satisfied, so what is poured must be you.

Taruṇāditya closes the verse by returning to the colour this whole tradition works in. Pāṭala is a pale red, rose or pink, the colour of the trumpet-flower the word also names. The first of the meditation verses that open this stotra begins by calling her aruṇā, the red of dawn, and the red appears again and again through the thousand names in the form of vermilion, hibiscus, coral, ruby and, six verses from here, the scarlet bandhūka blossom. The sun chosen is specifically taruṇa, young or tender, which is the sun of the first moments and not of noon. Whatever else this school is, it is committed to a single hue, and it keeps finding new objects in the world that carry it.
commentary.practice:
Both names in the first line open with caitanya, and the diphthong at the head of them is the first thing to get right. Ai is a full-length vowel in Sanskrit, worth two beats, not the quick glide of English eye. The c before it is a palatal affricate made with the tongue-body flat against the hard palate; English speakers produce something a little too far forward, closer to the ch of church. Aim it back and hold the vowel.

The hardest thing in the verse is the cluster in arghya: r, then an aspirated guttural gh, then the palatal glide y, three articulations with no vowel between them and the tongue travelling from a tap at the ridge to the soft palate to the hard palate. There is no way to acquire it except at half speed. Say ar, then ghya, then bring them together. You will meet the same cluster in the next verse in anarghya, so the work is not wasted.

Samārādhyā ends in dhy, a breathy dental stop into the palatal glide: one release, not d then h then y. This is the same ending as ārādhyā in the next verse and as several of the worship-names elsewhere in the hymn, and it is one of the most useful clusters in the text to fix properly.

In the second line, sadoditā contains a fusion you should be able to hear as a seam. Sadā ends in long ā and uditā begins with short u, and ā followed by u gives a single o. So the o in the middle of the word is where always meets risen. The very next name keeps sadā intact before a consonant, so the two names side by side show you the rule and its absence in the space of eight syllables.

Sadātuṣṭā gives the retroflex pair ṣṭ: the sibilant with the tongue-tip curled back, and the stop made in the same position without moving. Do not let the ṣ drift forward into an English sh. Then taruṇādityapāṭalā offers the other retroflex, ṭ in pāṭalā, and a ṇ in taruṇa that is retroflex for a purely mechanical reason — the r two syllables earlier has pulled it back. Once you know that rule, this name and vinivāriṇī in the previous verse stop looking arbitrary.

The metre is worth noticing here because the two lines are shaped so differently. The first is two names of eight syllables each; the second is four, four, eight. The caesura in both falls after the eighth syllable, which in the first line is inside the first name, between arghya and samārādhyā. Hear the pause without opening a gap in the sound.

In archanā, caitanyārghyasamārādhyāyai namaḥ is the longest dative in this part of the hymn and forces the rghy cluster and the dhy cluster into one breath. If you can produce it without slowing down, the verse holds no further difficulties.

What to hold while chanting it: the first two names are instructions, and they are not metaphors for sincerity. They say that what is being handed over in this rite is the awareness doing the handing. The three names that follow are there to tell you that the recipient does not need it.

171.subtitle: A slight smile, and a priceless gift

commentary.meaning: Four names, and the verse descends from method to result without a joint. It opens by refusing, for the second time in three verses, to choose between the two styles of practice — the same refusal as before, made now with the other pair of words. Then, with no transition at all, a face: the lotus of her face wearing the smallest possible smile, dara meaning only a little, so that the name specifies not a smile but the beginning of one. Then the vocabulary of the Kaula lineages, in which she is invoked as Kaulinī and is at the same time the one thing that stands unaccompanied. And then the longest of the four, which says what she gives: the station of absolute aloneness, and no price can be put on it. There is a small piece of wordplay running between this verse and the last. What was poured out there was arghya, from a root meaning to be worth; what is given here is an-arghya, past all reckoning of worth.
commentary.history:
Dakṣiṇa is one of the busiest words in Sanskrit. It means the right hand, and from that the south, which is on your right when you face the sunrise; it means favourable, straightforward, honest, and it is the standard word for the fee paid to a priest at the close of a rite. Every one of those senses is complimentary. The left has no comparable word of its own that is polite, and this name does not invent one: it forms its opposite by simple negation, adakṣiṇa, not-right. The usual term for the left-hand observance, vāma, is avoided. That avoidance is itself informative about how the tradition talks in a text meant for general recitation.

What the name asserts is that both kinds of practitioner reach her. The previous verse said the same with savya and apasavya, and saying it twice in three verses is not redundancy but emphasis at a structurally important place: the hymn is closing, and it is settling accounts on a question the tradition has never settled. That the question was live is easy to demonstrate from the commentarial literature on the Saundaryalaharī, where the two best-known interpreters take opposite views. Lakṣmīdhara reads the poem consistently as a document of the interior samaya way and is openly hostile to kaula practice; Bhāskararāya, a century or so later and the great commentator on this stotra, was associated with kaula lineages and reads accordingly. Two commentators, one text, and an argument about whether the rite has a body in it. The name in this verse does not adjudicate; it says both parties arrive.

Darasmera is a compound of two small words. Smera is from √smi, to smile, and dara used adverbially means a little, slightly, just. The result is not a description of cheerfulness but a precise measurement, and it belongs to a whole vocabulary of graded smiles in Sanskrit poetics — the smile that only shows in the eyes, the smile that parts the lips, the laugh that shows the teeth, the laugh that makes a sound. Sculptors worked to the same scale. The faces on the Cōḻa bronzes of this period are almost all set at the first or second degree, and the effect they aim for is not warmth but composure that could become warmth. That is what the name specifies.

Kula is the word this school's left wing takes its name from, and it is worth knowing how wide it is. In ordinary use it means a family, a clan, a herd, a lineage, a group of people who belong together. In Kaula usage it names the totality — the body, the senses, the energy of the practitioner, śakti as the whole manifest side of reality — and it is set against akula, the unmanifest, Śiva. A kaula is a member of that lineage and one who works with that totality rather than away from it. Kaulinī is the feminine, and the name has a second life worth noticing here: Kaulinī is also the name of one of the eight goddesses of speech whom the frame narrative credits with composing this very hymn. The last verse of the stotra will make that authorship explicit. Kevalā, standing next to it, is the ordinary adjective for alone, isolated, unmixed, pure — the same word used of unadulterated substances.

Kaivalya is the abstract noun formed from kevala, and it arrives here with a great deal of luggage. It is the standard term for liberation in Sāṃkhya and in classical Yoga, where it names the final isolation of consciousness from everything that is not consciousness, the two having been wrongly confused. That is a dualist's word, and its literal meaning is aloneness of a rather bleak kind. A nondualist Śākta hymn borrowing it has to mean something adjacent but not identical: not the separation of spirit from nature, since this text has spent nine hundred names insisting that nature is her, but the state of having nothing outside oneself with which to be compared. The commentators generally read kevala here in that second sense, and the reading is helped by the previous name, where kevalā is applied to her rather than to a liberated soul. Anarghya, priceless, is a-argha, without a price — the negation of the same word that gave the previous verse its guest-water. And pada is a station, a foothold, a place to stand, from the root that also gives the word for a foot: what is given is not an experience but a standing-place.
commentary.practice:
The first name is nine syllables and contains two sandhis of the same kind, one after the other. Dakṣiṇa ends in short a, adakṣiṇa begins with short a, and the two fuse into long ā; then adakṣiṇa ends in short a, ārādhyā begins with long ā, and short plus long again gives long ā. So both long vowels in the middle of dakṣiṇādakṣiṇārādhyā are seams, and the word means, cut at those seams, worshipped by the right-handed and by the not-right-handed alike.

That name also gives you kṣ twice. Sanskrit treats kṣ as a single cluster: a guttural k released directly into a retroflex ṣ, with the tongue-tip curling back for the sibilant. It is not the ksh of English cash-shop, and it is not two separate syllables. Say dakṣi twice at half speed before attempting the compound.

The second name has a fusion of its own — mukha, face, plus ambuja, lotus, giving mukhāmbuja, with the a and the a again producing ā. The kh in mukha is a genuinely aspirated guttural, k with breath after it, not the ch of German ach. Then mb, a labial nasal into its own stop, which is easy.

The third and fourth names are joined in writing by an avagraha, the small mark that looks like an S in the Devanagari text. It records an elision: kevalā ends in long ā, anarghya begins with short a, and a long ā followed by a short a swallows the a entirely. The mark tells you a vowel used to be there. It is not pronounced, and the two names run together as kevalānarghya. Reciters who try to sound the mark introduce a syllable the metre does not have.

Then anarghya brings back the cluster you met in the previous verse: r, aspirated gh, palatal y. Two verses in a row have handed you the same difficulty, which is as close as this hymn comes to setting an exercise. If arghya was manageable yesterday it will be manageable today.

Kaivalya has the full-length diphthong ai and then ly, a dental l running into the palatal glide. Padadāyinī at the end is all dentals and one of the easiest sequences in this part of the text; let it be a rest after the rest of the line.

In archanā the four become dakṣiṇādakṣiṇārādhyāyai namaḥ, darasmeramukhāmbujāyai namaḥ, kaulinīkevalāyai namaḥ and anarghyakaivalyapadadāyinyai namaḥ. The last is an ī-stem and takes -yai, which is worth attending to because -dāyinī names are common in this closing stretch and they all behave the same way.

What to hold while chanting it: the verse puts a smile in the middle of a doctrinal statement about eligibility and a doctrinal statement about liberation. That placement is the argument. Whatever the two schools do differently, and whatever aloneness turns out to mean, the thing they are both approaching is faintly amused.

crossReferences.relevance: The word the fourth name promises, in the text that defined it. Two things are worth noticing. Patañjali gives two formulations and joins them with or, which is unusual for a closing sūtra and suggests the term was already contested. And the second formulation, standing established in one's own form, is precisely what the previous verse of this hymn called her when it named her svasthā — so the stotra has already used the Yoga definition of liberation as a description of the goddess before it offers liberation as her gift.
